newsitem.title: CHINA: Economist urges end to China state sector dominance.
newsitem.headline: Economist urges end to China state sector dominance.

text.p: China's communist rulers must break free of taboos protecting the lumbering state sector and allow private enterprise to take a dominant role in the socialist economy, a senior economist said on Wednesday.

"The non-state sector as the mainstay of the economy has already become an objective fact in the economic life of our country," economist Cao Siyuan, who drafted China's bankruptcy law, told Reuters in an interview.

Cao's radical view comes as Communist Party leaders are locked in debate over the future of state-owned enterprise, the backbone of China's socialist system but which registered an unprecedented net loss in 1996.
Chinese officials have declined to put a figure on the year-end results for state enterprise last year, but insist performance has improved this year with an especially strong showing in May.
Vice Premier and economic tsar Zhu Rongji had pledged to extricate most of China's tens of thousands of state firms from their cycle of losses by 2000, the Xinhua news agency said.

Economists say that finding the courage to push ahead with unpalatable reforms of the flagging and long cosseted state sector will be a hot topic at a five-yearly Communist Party congress in late September or early October.
Cao stressed that it was now time for China to recognise the importance of the non-state sector in an economy that for four decades has been dominated by government-owned industry.

The strength of non-state enterprise -- a Chinese euphemism for the long-taboo private sector -- "already fits present economic rules and fits with the basic interests of the people, including workers of state-owned industry", Cao said.
"Recognising this beneficial change as a result of reform...and abandoning the slogan of 'taking the state-owned economy as the mainstay' is natural and rational," Cao said.
Cao backed his argument by citing official figures showing state-owned industry had declined to account for 33.9 percent of the total at end-1995 compared with 77.6 percent in 1978.
"This trend has continued in 1996 and 1997," he said.

The weak performance of state industry was closely linked to its ownership, Cao said, referring to one of the thorniest of ideological issues facing the leaders of a communist state in which assets are regarded as belonging to the proletariat.

"State-owned enterprise has an inherent weakness -- that is that it has not been able to individualise its ownership and so its profits and losses are not intimately linked to the material benefits of the people involved," Cao said.

"As a result, its economic strength must be rather weak," said Cao, director of the Beijing Siyuan Merger and Bankruptcy Consultancy. "This economic weakness means that the economic efficiency of state enterprise will be lower than that of the non-state sector."
In 1995, the non-state sector accounted for 31.2 percent of total fixed asset investment while its industrial output value accounted for 66.1 percent of the total, Cao said.
"One should feel pride in this and there is absolutely no reason to regard the non-state economy as something alien," Cao said, referring to lingering suspicion of the private sector.
Several senior economists have recently called for an end to one of the icons of communist rule, arguing that the dominance of the state sector should be abandoned in favour of profits.

China's leaders agree that tackling the state sector is among the most crucial reforms that remain to be implemented under late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's vision of a "socialist market economy".

Officials said state enterprise reform would be a priority this year, but progress has been slow amid fears bankruptcies would result in mass unemployment and social unrest -- anathema to China's communist leadership.
